Our Draft Survey service accurately measures cargo quantity on vessels before and after loading or discharge operations.

Ullage Survey

Our Bunker Survey service measures fuel quantity delivered to a vessel during bunkering. Our experienced marine surveyors conduct these surveys before and after operations

posts.html:
DUBAI, UAE – June 27, 2024 – Lox Quality Control and TIC Quality Control have jointly secured a contract with The Central Organization for Standardization and Quality Control (COSQC) in Iraq. The partnership will oversee the pre-inspection, testing, and issuance of certificates of conformity for goods imported into the Republic of Iraq.
The announcement was made during a high-profile event held at the Fairmont Hotel in Dubai. Key presenters of VOC program are Osama Al Kilani, Business Development Manager of TIC Quality Control, Majd Nassri, Operation Manager at TIC Quality Control, and Mohammed Hassan Mahmood, CEO of Lox Quality Control. The event was attended by the Commercial Attaché representative of the Consulate General of the Republic of Iraq in Dubai as well as delegates from commercial and trading companies exporting to the Republic of Iraq.


The partnership between Lox and TIC Quality Control will play an important role in maintaining and enhancing the quality standards of goods entering Iraq. Their responsibilities will encompass a comprehensive range of services, from initial pre-inspection to final certification, ensuring that all imported goods meet the rigorous standards set by the Iraqi government.
During the presentation, the speakers elaborated on the certification of conformity program and its importance in regulating Iraq’s import market. They also highlighted how the collaboration between Lox and TIC Quality Control would streamline the certification process, potentially facilitating smoother international trade with Iraq.
The event concluded with optimism this program marks a significant step in Iraq’s efforts to standardize and control the quality of imported goods, potentially impacting various sectors of the Iraqi econom.

posts.title: Iraqi Quality Mark – COSQC Regulation Update
posts.excerpt: A mark issued by the Central Organization for Standardization and Quality Control (COSQC) after the approval of the Minister of Planning, indicating the conformity of products to their specific Iraqi Standard Specification. This mark is granted in accordance with the Iraqi Quality Mark Instructions No. (2) of 2011, published in the Iraqi Gazette, issue No. […]
posts.html:
A mark issued by the Central Organization for Standardization and Quality Control (COSQC) after the approval of the Minister of Planning, indicating the conformity of products to their specific Iraqi Standard Specification. This mark is granted in accordance with the Iraqi Quality Mark Instructions No. (2) of 2011, published in the Iraqi Gazette, issue No. 4179 on 07/03/2011.
Based on the decision of the Ministerial Council for Economy No. (230339 Q), communicated through their letter No. (2311066) on 06/12/2023, it is required for (parent) manufacturing companies to obtain the Iraqi Quality Mark for their products supplied to Iraq, as listed below:
✔ Household Storage Electrical Water Heaters
✔ Household Electric room heaters
✔ Household Electric Refrigeration Appliances (Refrigerator, Refrigerator – Freezer, Freezer)
✔ Household Air Conditioners
✔ Electric ovens
✔ Cigarettes
If you require guidance through the process of obtaining the Iraqi Quality Mark, please do not hesitate to contact us at +971 50 6242612/+971 50 436 7933 or email voc@ticqc.ae. We look forward to assisting you!

posts.html:
TICQC was honored to participate in the Global Kabuli Chana Conference 2026, organized by the Kabuli Chana Traders Association (KCTA). The prestigious event was held on February 22, 2026, at the Grand Hall of Brilliant Convention Centre in Indore.

As one of India’s leading agricultural trade hubs, Indore provided the ideal setting for this high-impact global gathering. The conference brought together international traders, exporters, suppliers, brokers, policymakers, and key stakeholders from across the global pulse industry.

The event was also supported by the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), further highlighting its national and international significance within India’s Agri-export ecosystem

A Historic Milestone for Indian Agri-Trade

The Global Kabuli Chana Conference 2026 marked a significant achievement for India’s agricultural export sector.

KCTA extended its heartfelt gratitude to Hon’ble Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, respected Ministers, MLAs, APEDA officials, and more than 800 distinguished delegates whose presence and support made the conference a monumental success.

Participants experienced insightful knowledge sessions, meaningful discussions on global trade developments, and valuable networking opportunities

Together, we are taking India to the World.

The Growing Importance of Kabuli Chana in Global Agricultural Trade

Kabuli chana (chickpeas) continues to play a vital role in international agricultural commerce, with strong and expanding demand across the Middle East, Europe, Africa, and Asia.
As global trade volumes increase, exporters must meet evolving international requirements, including:

  • Quality grading and product specifications
  • Moisture content compliance
  • Phytosanitary certification
  • Food safety regulations
  • Pre-shipment inspection standards

Compliance with destination-country regulations is essential to minimizing commercial risks, preventing shipment rejections, and safeguarding buyer confidence. This is where independent third-party inspection and quality assurance services become critical.

Key Conference Discussions Shaping the Future of Pulse Trade

The conference addressed several pressing issues impacting the global pulse sector:

  • Global production and consumption trends
  • Supply chain and logistics challenges
  • International export compliance frameworks
  • Market price outlook and demand forecasts
  • Risk management strategies in agricultural exports

For TICQC, the event provided an excellent opportunity to engage directly with exporters and traders seeking dependable inspection, testing, and certification services to strengthen their international operations.

TICQC’s Commitment to Supporting Global Pulse Exporters

As a trusted third-party inspection and quality control company, TICQC is dedicated to helping exporters, traders, and suppliers meet stringent international trade standards. Our specialized services for the agricultural and pulse sector include:

  • Pre-shipment inspection
  • Quality and quantity verification
  • Loading and container supervision
  • Sampling and laboratory testing coordination
  • Destination-market compliance verification

Through active participation in global industry events, TICQC continues to strengthen international partnerships and stay aligned with evolving regulatory requirements and quality expectations.

Indore: A Strategic Hub for the Pulse Industry

Indore is widely recognized as one of India’s premier centers for agricultural commodities and pulse trading. Hosting the conference at the Brilliant Convention Centre provided a central, well-connected venue for both domestic and international delegates. The region’s deep integration with pulse production, processing, and trade makes it a natural platform for global collaboration and industry advancement.

Driving Sustainable and Secure Global Trade

TICQC’s participation in the Global Kabuli Chana Conference 2026 reflects our ongoing commitment to promoting secure, transparent, and compliant global trade operations. As international demand for Kabuli chana continues to rise, collaboration among exporters, traders, regulators, and independent inspection agencies will remain essential to:

  • Reduce commercial risks
  • Ensure shipment compliance
  • Protect buyer confidence
  • Maintain consistent product quality

TICQC remains committed to facilitating smoother cross-border transactions through reliable inspection, testing, and certification services, supporting India’s growing presence in the global agricultural marketplace.

TIC Quality Control at AAHAR 2026: Exploring Opportunities in the Global Food and Hospitality Industry

The team from TIC Quality Control recently attended the AAHAR. The International Food & Hospitality Fair, one of the most influential trade exhibitions in the food and hospitality industry. The 40th edition of the event took place from 10–14 March 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. Over the course of five days, the exhibition brought together food manufacturers, hospitality businesses, exporters, technology providers, and global buyers under one roof. The event served as a major networking platform where industry professionals explored innovations, built partnerships, and exchanged insights about emerging trends shaping the global food ecosystem.

For TIC Quality Control attending AAHAR 2026 provided an excellent opportunity to interact with industry stakeholders, understand the latest developments in food production and hospitality services, and strengthen relationships with businesses seeking quality assurance and inspection services. As global supply chains continue to expand, events like AAHAR create a space where companies can collaborate and discover solutions that support safe, compliant, and high-quality food production.

What is AAHAR – The International Food & Hospitality Fair?

AAHAR is widely recognized as one of Asia’s leading B2B trade exhibitions dedicated to the food processing, food service, and hospitality industries. The exhibition is organized by the India Trade Promotion Organisation under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, in collaboration with the Ministry of Food Processing Industries. Over the past four decades, the event has evolved into a global platform connecting businesses across the food supply chain—from farmers and manufacturers to distributors, hospitality providers, and international buyers.

The 2026 edition marked the 40th anniversary of AAHAR, highlighting the event’s long-standing contribution to the growth of the food and hospitality sector in India and beyond. Each year, the exhibition attracts thousands of professionals from across the world who come together to showcase new products, technologies, and services. The event is designed primarily as a business-to-business (B2B) platform, allowing companies to build partnerships, explore export opportunities, and expand into new markets.

AAHAR 2026 was one of the largest editions of the event to date. The exhibition featured over 1,800 exhibitors, including 155 international participants from 17 countries, and was expected to attract more than 100,000 business visitors during the five-day event. These participants represented diverse sectors such as processed foods, beverages, dairy products, spices, bakery items, hospitality equipment, kitchen technology, and packaging solutions.

Another major highlight of AAHAR 2026 was the participation of Italy as the partner country, marking the first time the event featured an official partner nation. This collaboration highlighted the growing international interest in India’s expanding food processing and hospitality industries.

Key Highlights and Exhibitions at AAHAR 2026

AAHAR is not just a traditional exhibition; it is a comprehensive industry platform designed to showcase innovation and foster collaboration across the global food ecosystem. The exhibition was spread across multiple halls at Bharat Mandapam, covering more than 115,000 square meters of exhibition space and featuring specialized pavilions dedicated to different sectors of the industry.

posts.title: What Rising Grain Export Inspections Reveal About Global Trade in 2026
posts.excerpt: Numbers tell stories. And right now, the numbers coming out of global grain export inspections data are telling a story worth paying close attention to whether you are a grain trader, an importer, a logistics operator, or anyone else with a stake in how agricultural commodities move around the world. For the week ending March […]
posts.html:
Numbers tell stories. And right now, the numbers coming out of global grain export inspections data are telling a story worth paying close attention to whether you are a grain trader, an importer, a logistics operator, or anyone else with a stake in how agricultural commodities move around the world.

For the week ending March 12, 2026, corn export inspections in the United States totalled 1.65 million metric tons, up from 1.52 million metric tons the previous week. Soybean inspections came in at 966,000 metric tons, rising from 887,000 metric tons a week earlier and meaningfully higher than the 664,000 metric tons recorded during the same week in 2025. Wheat inspections, meanwhile, fell to 343,000 metric tons, down from 498,000 metric tons the prior week.

These weekly figures are more than just statistics. They reflect the actual physical movement of grain from origin facilities, through inspection and toward export and when you zoom out to look at the full marketing year picture, the shifts in direction become even more significant.

The Bigger Picture: What Marketing Year Data Reveals

Weekly inspection figures capture a snapshot, but marketing year totals show the real momentum. As of mid-March 2026, the USDA had inspected 42.86 million metric tons of corn since the start of the marketing year a figure that is tracking meaningfully higher than the same period last year. Sorghum has seen even more dramatic growth, with year-to-date shipments running approximately 61% above last year’s pace.

On the other side of the ledger, soybeans are under pressure. Marketing year-to-date soybean inspections stand at 28.06 million metric tons, lower than the equivalent figure from a year ago. Wheat, despite a softer recent week, is running about 3 million metric tons above last year’s year-to-date total at 19.47 million metric tons inspected.

What does this split picture mean? It reflects a global feed grain market that is in strong demand, corn and sorghum are both key inputs for livestock feed, and their outperformance suggests that animal agriculture around the world is drawing heavily on export supplies. Soybeans, by contrast, are facing a more complex demand environment, with buyers weighing prices, logistics, and the availability of supply from competing origins.

Why Export Inspection Data Matters and What It Actually Measures

Before going further, it is worth explaining what export inspection data actually captures, because it is often misunderstood.

In the United States, the Federal Grain Inspection Service (FGIS) part of the USDA is responsible for official grain inspection and weighing at export facilities. When a shipment of corn, soybeans, sorghum, or wheat is prepared for export, it must be officially inspected and weighed before it can leave the country. This is not optional, and it is not a formality. It is a mandatory, standardised process that certifies the grade, quality, moisture content, weight, and condition of the grain.

The weekly inspection data published by the USDA reflects the volume of grain that has gone through this process at export facilities across the country, primarily at Gulf of Mexico terminals, Pacific Northwest ports, and Great Lakes facilities. The Gulf handles the majority of corn, soybean, and sorghum shipments, while the Pacific Northwest is the dominant channel for grain moving into Asian markets.

Every metric ton counted in those weekly figures represents grain that has been sampled, tested, graded, and certified. It represents documentation that exists. And it represents a standard that both the exporter and the importer are relying on.

The Role of Inspection in Protecting Both Sides of a Grain Trade

In global agricultural commodity trade, grain inspection is not just a regulatory requirement at the point of export, it is a commercial tool that protects both the seller and the buyer.

For exporters, official inspection certification establishes what was shipped. It records the grade, moisture, protein content where applicable, weight, and condition of the cargo at the moment it left the origin facility. If a dispute arises at the destination, if the buyer claims the grain arrived short in weight, below grade, or contaminated, the exporter’s position begins with the inspection certificate issued at origin. Without it, the exporter has no documentary defence.

For importers and end users feed mills, grain processors, food manufacturers, the inspection certificate is the first assurance that what they ordered is what they are receiving. When an importer specifies US No. 2 Yellow Corn with a maximum moisture content of 14% and maximum aflatoxin levels within safe limits, the export inspection certificate is the document confirming those specifications were met when the grain was loaded.

This is not merely theoretical. Grain shipment disputes are a regular feature of international commodity trade, and the most common underlying cause of a dispute is a gap between what was contracted, what was shipped, and what arrived. Inspection done properly, at the right point in the chain, by qualified professionals, is the mechanism that closes those gaps.

Competition Is Growing: What That Means for Inspection Standards

One of the most notable developments in grain export markets right now is the re-emergence of strong competition from other origins. Argentina and Ukraine are both active in the corn export market, offering supply to buyers who might otherwise turn to the United States. Brazil remains a dominant force in soybeans.

This competition is relevant to inspection standards in a practical way. When buyers have multiple origins to choose from, they can be, and increasingly are, selective about documentation quality, not just price. A buyer choosing between US-origin and Argentine-origin corn is not only comparing prices per metric ton. They are comparing the reliability of the supply chain, the quality of the inspection documentation, and their confidence that what was contracted will be what arrives.

Markets where competition is intense tend to raise standards over time, because sellers who cannot provide credible, independent quality documentation lose business to those who can. This is a dynamic that is playing out across global grain markets right now, and it is particularly relevant for buyers and sellers operating in markets where official export inspection is not as standardised as in the United States.

What Grain Buyers in Importing Countries Should Be Checking

For importers receiving grain shipments, whether corn, soybeans, sorghum, or wheat, the export inspection certificate issued at origin is the starting point, but it should not be the only check in the system. There are several key considerations that determine whether a shipment arriving at destination will match what the documentation says.

Transit time and storage conditions matter. Grain that was inspected and certified at a US Gulf terminal in compliance with all specifications can still arrive in poor condition if it was stowed improperly, exposed to moisture during the voyage, or held in a vessel with inadequate ventilation. Export inspection certifies condition at the point of loading, not at the point of arrival.

Aflatoxin and mycotoxin levels can change in transit. This is particularly relevant for corn, which is susceptible to mould growth if temperature and moisture conditions during the voyage are not controlled. A corn shipment that tested within safe aflatoxin limits at origin can breach acceptable levels by the time it arrives at a destination port if transit conditions allowed mould to develop. Destination inspection is the only way to establish what the cargo’s condition is on arrival.

Weight can vary. Grain absorbs and releases moisture during a voyage, meaning the weight at destination may differ from the weight at loading. This is a well-understood feature of bulk grain shipments and is typically accounted for by contract, but the only way to establish the actual delivered weight is to weigh the cargo at discharge.

Grade characteristics can shift. Factors like broken kernels, foreign matter, and heat-damaged grain can increase during a voyage, particularly in poor storage conditions. A shipment that graded as US No. 2 at loading may present differently on arrival.

For these reasons, many sophisticated importers arrange for independent third-party inspection at both origin and destination, giving them a documented record of the cargo’s condition at each end of the journey, and a clear basis for establishing where in the supply chain any discrepancy originated.

Sorghum’s Surge: A Market Worth Watching

The 61% year-over-year increase in sorghum export inspections is worth noting specifically, because it is a commodity that receives less attention than corn, soybeans, or wheat but is growing rapidly in global trade.

Sorghum is primarily traded as a feed grain, and its growth in export volumes reflects strong demand from livestock industries in key importing countries. It is drought-resistant, which makes it an attractive crop for producers in certain growing regions, and it is gluten-free, which has created modest demand in specialty food markets beyond its traditional use in animal feed.

For traders and importers dealing with sorghum, the inspection considerations are broadly similar to corn, moisture, aflatoxin levels, foreign matter, and weight are the key parameters but sorghum’s different physical characteristics mean that sampling and testing protocols must be adapted accordingly.

The Broader Context: Global Trade Pressure and the Value of Trust

The grain market in early 2026 is navigating a complex environment. The US stock market remains under pressure, with the Dow trading below 46,000. Farmer selling is reportedly slowing as basis levels steady. Private estimates for the March 31 USDA Prospective Plantings report suggest corn acres in the range of 94 to 95 million, a figure that will help define supply expectations for the coming marketing year.

Against this backdrop, the function of inspection in global trade is not merely technical, it is about trust. Buyers and sellers who have never met, operating across different legal jurisdictions, time zones, and languages, rely on standardised inspection documentation to establish a shared, objective record of what was traded. When that documentation is credible, disputes are resolved faster. When it is not, they become expensive, time-consuming, and damaging to commercial relationships.

In a market where volumes are rising as corn and sorghum inspection data currently shows the pressure on quality assurance systems increases too. More shipments, moving faster, through competitive markets, mean less room for documentation gaps or quality surprises.

How TIC Quality Control Supports Grain and Commodity Trade

TIC Quality Control provides commodity inspection services for agricultural products including grains and oilseeds, with operations across key trading origins and destinations. Our services for grain and commodity shipments include pre-shipment quality and quantity inspection, loading supervision, discharge inspection at destination, weight and moisture verification, and sampling for laboratory testing.

For importers and traders receiving grain shipments, we provide independent assessment of cargo condition on arrival establishing the facts on the ground in a form that is accepted by buyers, sellers, banks, and trade finance institutions. For exporters and shippers, we provide pre-shipment documentation that protects your position in the event of destination disputes.

In a market as data-driven and volume-sensitive as global grain trade, the value of independent, professional inspection is not an overhead, it is a commercial safeguard that pays for itself the first time it prevents a dispute, protects a payment, or resolves a discrepancy before it becomes a legal claim.

TIC Quality Control Gandhidham provides commodity inspection and quality assurance services for agricultural products including grains and oilseeds, supporting clients across key global trade routes with a strong operational presence in Gandhidham, India. From pre-shipment inspection and loading supervision to laboratory testing and certification, our team ensures that every cargo meets contractual specifications before it leaves origin. We work closely with exporters, traders, and logistics operators to create reliable documentation that protects commercial interests and reduces the risk of disputes in international trade.

With expanding operations in Dubai, UAE, TIC Quality Control also supports importers and end users at destination by delivering independent inspection, discharge supervision, and cargo verification services. This dual presence across origin and destination markets allows us to provide a complete, transparent view of cargo condition throughout the supply chain, strengthening trust and consistency in global commodity movements.

posts.title: What is a Certificate of Conformity (CoC)?
posts.excerpt: If you are involved in manufacturing, importing, or exporting goods, you have almost certainly come across the term Certificate of Conformity, or CoC. It appears on customs checklists, supplier contracts, and regulatory documents. Yet many businesses still do not fully understand what it is, why it is required, or what happens if they do not […]
posts.html:
If you are involved in manufacturing, importing, or exporting goods, you have almost certainly come across the term Certificate of Conformity, or CoC. It appears on customs checklists, supplier contracts, and regulatory documents. Yet many businesses still do not fully understand what it is, why it is required, or what happens if they do not have one.

This guide answers all of those questions in plain, practical language. Whether you are new to compliance or looking to sharpen your knowledge before entering markets like Iraq, Egypt, or Libya, this article covers everything you need to know about the Certificate of Conformity.

Certificate of Conformity: The Basic Definition

A Certificate of Conformity (CoC) is an official document that confirms a product, process, or service meets a defined set of standards or regulatory requirements. It is typically issued by an accredited third-party inspection or certification body after the product has been assessed through testing, inspection, or audit.

Think of it as a formal written guarantee that says: this product has been checked and it meets the required standards. The certificate references specific regulations or technical specifications, and it identifies the body responsible for making that determination.

The standards referenced in a CoC can be international, such as ISO standards; regional, such as Arab technical regulations; or country-specific regulations set by national standards bodies in the destination market.

Why is a Certificate of Conformity Important?

A CoC is not just paperwork. It has real commercial and legal significance. Here is why it matters:

•        Protects Consumer Safety: The primary purpose of conformity standards is to keep people safe. Products that do not meet safety requirements can cause injury, illness, or environmental damage. A CoC provides documented evidence that proper testing has taken place.

•        Enables Market Access: Many countries require a valid CoC before goods can clear customs. In Iraq, Egypt, and Libya, regulated products cannot legally enter the market without certification from an approved body. Without this document, shipments can be delayed, rejected, or returned at the port.

•        Demonstrates Legal Compliance: Manufacturers and importers are legally required to meet local and international standards. A CoC is proof of that compliance, which reduces exposure to fines, recalls, and legal liability.

•        Speeds Up Customs Clearance: Well-documented shipments with valid CoCs clear customs faster. This reduces storage costs, prevents supply chain disruptions, and builds confidence between trading partners.

•        Builds Business Credibility: Companies that obtain CoCs consistently signal a genuine commitment to quality. Over time, this strengthens relationships with buyers, distributors, and regulators.

Types of Certificates of Conformity

Not every Certificate of Conformity looks or functions the same. The type required depends on the product, the destination market, and the applicable regulatory framework. Here are the main categories:

1. Manufacturer’s Certificate of Conformity (MCoC)

This is a self-declaration issued by the manufacturer, confirming that their product meets the specified standards. It is generally quicker and less expensive to obtain since it does not involve an independent assessment. However, it carries less credibility in regulated markets because no third party has verified the claims.

2. Third-Party Certificate of Conformity

Issued by an independent, accredited testing or inspection organisation, this is the most widely recognised and trusted form of CoC in international trade. The certifying body evaluates the product against relevant standards and issues the certificate based on its own findings. Markets like Iraq, Egypt, and Libya require or strongly prefer third-party certification for regulated product categories.

3. Government or Regulatory Body Certificate

In certain cases, a government authority or national standards body directly issues a CoC following product assessment. These certificates carry formal legal authority in their respective jurisdictions and are often mandatory for specific product types.

4. Shipment-Specific Certificate of Conformity

Some importing countries require a separate CoC for every individual shipment rather than a single certificate covering a product type. This ensures that each consignment leaving the factory has been inspected before export, reducing the risk of substandard or counterfeit goods entering the market.

Which Industries Require a Certificate of Conformity?

Almost any product category can require conformity certification, but certain industries depend on it as a core part of their compliance framework:

•        Electrical and Electronic Equipment: Appliances, cables, lighting products, and consumer electronics must meet electrical safety and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) standards.

•        Construction Materials: Steel, cement, pipes, and other structural materials require CoCs to confirm they meet load-bearing and fire resistance specifications.

•        Automotive Parts and Vehicles: Vehicle components must comply with road safety regulations in the destination country.

•        Medical Devices and Healthcare Products: These carry some of the strictest conformity requirements given the direct impact on patient safety.

•        Food Contact Materials and Packaging: Containers, wrapping, and processing equipment must meet hygiene and food safety standards.

•        Chemical and Hazardous Materials: Handling, labelling, and transport of chemicals require compliance documentation.

•        Toys and Children’s Products: Material composition, mechanical hazards, and flammability all fall under detailed safety standards.

•        Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Safety helmets, gloves, respiratory protection, and similar items require certification before sale.

What Information Does a Certificate of Conformity Include?

The exact content varies by issuing body and applicable standard, but a complete and valid Certificate of Conformity typically contains the following:

•        Full name and contact details of the manufacturer or supplier

•        Name and address of the importer or buyer where applicable

•        Detailed product description including model numbers, batch references, and technical specifications

•        The specific standards or regulations with which the product complies

•        Testing and inspection methods used during assessment

•        Results and findings from the evaluation

•        Date of issue and certificate validity period

•        Name, accreditation number, and authorised signature of the issuing body

•        A unique certificate reference number for tracking and verification purposes

Accuracy matters enormously. Any mismatch between the CoC and the actual shipment can trigger customs holds, rejection of goods, or questions about the authenticity of the documentation.

How to Obtain a Certificate of Conformity: Step by Step

The process of obtaining a CoC follows a clear sequence. While the details vary by product and destination market, the general steps are:

•        Step 1: Identify the Applicable Standards: Start by determining which standards apply to your product in the target market. This involves understanding both the product category and the regulatory environment of the country you are exporting to.

•        Step 2: Choose an Accredited Certification Body: Select a recognised and accredited inspection or testing organisation. Verify that they hold accreditation from a reputable national or international body and are accepted by the relevant market authorities.

•        Step 3: Prepare and Submit Technical Documentation: Provide the certification body with all relevant product documentation, including design specifications, material data sheets, manufacturing process details, and any previous test reports.

•        Step 4: Testing and Inspection: The product is evaluated against the applicable standards. This may involve laboratory testing, chemical analysis, performance testing, or on-site factory audits, depending on the product type and standard.

•        Step 5: Review and Certificate Issuance: If your product meets all requirements, the certification body issues the Certificate of Conformity. If it does not, you will need to address any non-conformities and arrange a re-assessment before the certificate can be issued.

•        Step 6: Maintain Ongoing Compliance: A CoC is not a one-time achievement. Standards are updated, products are revised, and certificates have expiry dates. Businesses must monitor these changes and renew certification as required to remain compliant.

Certificate of Conformity Requirements in Iraq, Egypt and Libya

For businesses exporting to Iraq, Egypt, and Libya, understanding the conformity certification requirements of each market is essential before goods reach the border.

Iraq

Iraq operates a mandatory Conformity Assessment Programme (CAP) that came into effect in January 2020. Under this programme, a Certificate of Conformity is required for a wide range of regulated product categories before goods can enter the Iraqi market. Covered categories include electrical and electronic appliances, food products, toys, vehicle spare parts, chemicals, cosmetics, construction materials, and textiles. Every shipment of regulated goods must be accompanied by a CoC issued by an approved certification body in the country of export. Shipments arriving without a valid CoC are rejected at Iraqi customs. Additionally, certain electrical products must carry the Iraqi Quality Mark (IQM) as an added layer of compliance.

Egypt

Egypt enforces a mandatory pre-shipment inspection programme for a broad range of imported goods. Regulated products cannot enter the Egyptian market without a Certificate of Inspection issued by an approved third-party body before the goods leave the country of origin. Product categories subject to conformity requirements in Egypt include electrical and electronic devices, textiles, footwear, leather goods, cosmetics, and food contact materials. Products must also carry Arabic labelling that includes the manufacturer’s name, product description, country of origin, and other required information. The inspection certificate is valid for one year from the date of issue.

Libya

In Libya, all goods exported under a Letter of Credit require a Certificate of Inspection issued by a recognised inspection company, as mandated by the Central Bank of Libya. The inspection must be carried out in the country of export before shipment, and the certificate must be presented to the importer for customs clearance on arrival. Where no Libya-specific standard exists, internationally recognised standards are applied. Product markings and instructions must be provided in Arabic, and certain prohibited categories are strictly not permitted entry.

Across all three markets, regulations are subject to change and enforcement is taken seriously. Businesses are strongly advised to verify current requirements before each shipment and to work with a certification body that has active, up-to-date knowledge of these markets.

Common Misconceptions About Certificates of Conformity

Several misunderstandings regularly cause problems for businesses dealing with CoC requirements. Here are the most common ones worth addressing:

•        A CoC is the same as a quality certificate. Not quite. A CoC confirms that a specific product meets a specific standard. A quality certificate such as ISO 9001 covers a company’s overall quality management system. Both are valuable, but they are different instruments serving different purposes.

•        Once certified, a product stays certified. Standards evolve, regulations are updated, and certificates have expiry dates. A CoC obtained several years ago may no longer reflect current requirements, which could leave your business exposed.

•        A supplier’s self-declaration is always acceptable. In many regulated markets and for high-risk product categories, a manufacturer’s self-declaration does not satisfy regulatory requirements. Independent third-party certification is required.

•        One CoC covers all markets. A certificate obtained for one country does not automatically satisfy the requirements of another. Iraq, Egypt, and Libya each operate their own regulatory frameworks, and separate certification may be needed for each destination.

•        CoC requirements only apply to large manufacturers. Requirements are determined by product category and destination market, not by company size. Small and medium-sized businesses importing regulated goods face the same obligations as large corporations.

How Accredited Inspection Bodies Support CoC Certification

The value of a Certificate of Conformity is only as strong as the organisation that issues it. Accredited inspection and testing bodies play a critical role in global trade by providing independent, impartial product assessments that both buyers and regulators can trust.

Accreditation is the formal recognition that a certification body has demonstrated its technical competence to carry out specific assessments. National and international accreditation frameworks provide this recognition, ensuring that certified products are assessed to a consistent and verifiable standard.

When selecting a certification partner, businesses should confirm that the body holds accreditation from a recognised authority, has hands-on experience in the relevant product category, and is formally accepted by the authorities in the target market. Choosing the right partner from the outset can prevent costly delays, failed inspections, and compliance gaps.

Frequently Asked Questions About Certificates of Conformity

How long is a Certificate of Conformity valid?

Validity periods vary depending on the issuing body and the applicable standard. In Egypt, the inspection certificate is valid for one year. In Iraq, CoCs are typically issued per shipment. Always confirm the validity period with your certification body and build renewal reminders into your compliance calendar.

Is a Certificate of Conformity the same as a CE certificate?

No. CE marking is a specific conformity marking required for products sold in the European Economic Area (EEA). A CE certificate is one type of CoC. Other markets have their own conformity marks and certification schemes. Iraq, Egypt, and Libya each operate separate and independent conformity frameworks.

Can a Certificate of Conformity be rejected at customs?

Yes. Customs authorities can reject a CoC if the issuing body is not recognised in the destination market, if the certificate does not reference the correct standards, if the product description does not match the shipment, or if the certificate has expired. Working with an accredited and recognised certification body is the best way to avoid rejection.

What is the difference between a CoC and a test report?

A test report documents the results of specific laboratory tests conducted on a product. A Certificate of Conformity is the formal declaration, backed by those test results, that the product meets the required standards. The test report supports the CoC but is not a substitute for it.

Final Thoughts

A Certificate of Conformity is one of the most important documents in product compliance and international trade. It connects regulatory requirements with commercial reality, giving buyers, customs authorities, and consumers confidence that a product is safe, legal, and accurately represented.

For businesses exporting to Iraq, Egypt, and Libya, the CoC process requires careful attention. Standards differ by product type, regulations change regularly, and the consequences of non-compliance can include shipment rejection, financial penalties, and reputational damage. Getting this right from the start is always the better approach.

Nigeria Rice Trade Window 2026: A Timely opportunity for Global Exporters

The global rice trade is witnessing a significant shift in April 2026 as Nigeria opens a new import window following major policy adjustments. For exporters, traders, and agri-commodity businesses, this development is not just another update. It is a time-sensitive commercial opportunity that demands close attention and quick strategic action.

Nigeria has long been one of the largest rice-consuming countries in Africa. However, strict import policies and high duties in recent years limited direct trade flows, encouraging informal routes through neighboring countries. With the latest reduction in import duties, the situation is changing rapidly, creating a more structured and potentially profitable trade environment.

Understanding the Policy Shift

The Nigerian government has reduced import duties on rice significantly. Previously, rice imports faced duties of around 70 percent, making direct imports commercially unviable for many traders. Now, the duty has been reduced to approximately 47.5 percent. Even more notable is the reduction in duties on broken rice, which has dropped to around 30 percent.

This is a major shift. Such reductions directly impact landed cost, allowing importers to compete more effectively in the local market. For exporters, this opens the door to re-enter a market that was previously difficult to access through formal trade channels.

What Triggered This Change

To understand the opportunity, it is important to look at the broader economic context in Nigeria. The country has been facing rising food inflation, which has put pressure on both consumers and policymakers. One of the key contributing factors has been the removal of fuel subsidies, which increased transportation and production costs across the supply chain.

As rice is a staple food in Nigeria, any price increase directly affects millions of households. The government, under pressure to stabilize food prices and ensure availability, has responded by easing import restrictions. This move is aimed at increasing supply in the domestic market and controlling inflation.

Why This Matters for Exporters

From a global trade perspective, Nigeria’s decision is highly significant. It signals a temporary but powerful demand surge in one of Africa’s largest markets. Exporters who were previously hesitant due to high duties may now find viable margins, especially in the broken rice segment where price sensitivity is higher.

In addition, buyers in Nigeria are expected to actively explore new sourcing options to take advantage of the revised duty structure. This creates immediate demand for competitive suppliers who can deliver both quality and price efficiency.

However, this is not just about supply. Timing, compliance, and execution will play a critical role in determining success. The market is opening, but it is not fully liberalized, which means risks still exist.

A Window, Not a Permanent Shift

One of the most important aspects of this opportunity is its temporary nature. Policy changes in Nigeria can be dynamic, and reversals are not uncommon. This means exporters must approach this opportunity with a strategic mindset rather than assuming long-term stability.

Those who act early may benefit from stronger relationships, better pricing, and first-mover advantage. On the other hand, delays could result in missed opportunities or exposure to sudden policy changes.

In the next part, we will explore the real market dynamics on the ground, including buyer behavior, demand trends, and key risks that every exporter must understand before entering this market.

Nigeria Rice Trade Window 2026: Market Dynamics, Demand Trends, and Ground Realities

While the recent reduction in import duties has created a strong entry point into the Nigerian rice market, understanding the on-ground realities is essential before making any trade decisions. The opportunity is real, but so are the complexities. Exporters who combine speed with market awareness will be in the best position to succeed.

Current Market Demand in Nigeria

Nigeria remains one of the largest consumers of rice in Africa, with demand consistently outpacing domestic production. Despite government efforts to boost local farming, supply gaps have persisted, especially in urban centers where consumption levels are high.

With the latest policy shift, buyers are expected to return to the international market with renewed interest. In particular, there is likely to be strong demand for broken rice. This segment caters to price-sensitive consumers and industrial users, making it highly responsive to changes in import duties.

Early signals from trade circles suggest that Nigerian importers are actively evaluating pricing, logistics options, and supplier reliability. The demand is not theoretical. It is already building, and suppliers who are prepared can start engaging immediately.

Buyer Behavior and Expectations

Nigerian buyers are experienced and highly price-conscious. They are quick to respond to favorable policy changes but equally cautious when it comes to execution risks. This means exporters must be ready to offer competitive pricing along with clear, transparent terms.

Speed of response is also critical. In a fast-moving market like this, delayed communication or slow negotiations can result in lost deals. Buyers are likely to work with partners who can provide quick quotations, flexible shipment options, and reliable timelines.

Another important factor is consistency in quality. Nigerian importers have faced challenges in the past with inconsistent shipments, so trust and reliability will play a major role in building long-term relationships.

The Reality of a Semi-Open Market

Despite the positive signals, it is important to recognize that the Nigerian rice market is not fully open. The current policy environment can be described as controlled flexibility rather than complete liberalization.

Import regulations may still involve documentation requirements, compliance checks, and administrative processes that can vary over time. Exporters must stay updated with the latest guidelines and ensure that all shipments meet regulatory standards.

There is also the possibility of sudden policy adjustments. The government’s primary goal is to stabilize domestic prices, and once that objective is achieved, import duties or restrictions could be revised again.

Risks That Cannot Be Ignored

Entering this market without proper safeguards can expose traders to several risks. Policy reversals remain the most significant concern. A sudden increase in duties or a change in import rules could impact profitability or delay shipments.

Currency fluctuations are another factor to consider. Exchange rate volatility can affect both pricing and payment terms, making it important to structure contracts carefully.

Logistics and clearance challenges may also arise, especially for those unfamiliar with Nigerian ports and procedures. Delays at ports, documentation issues, or unexpected charges can impact overall trade efficiency.

The Importance of Strategic Execution

Given these dynamics, exporters should approach Nigeria with a balanced strategy. This includes conducting due diligence on buyers, securing clear contractual terms, and working with experienced logistics partners.

Rather than treating this as a routine export market, it should be seen as a high-potential but time-sensitive opportunity that requires careful planning. Those who understand the ground realities will be able to navigate challenges while maximizing returns.

In the next part, we will focus on how exporters can practically enter this market, including trade routes, pricing strategies, and execution models that can help convert this opportunity into real business.

Nigeria Rice Trade Window 2026: Entry Strategies, Trade Routes, and Execution Planning

With demand building and policy conditions temporarily favorable, the next step for exporters is clear: execution. However, entering the Nigerian market successfully requires more than just identifying an opportunity. It demands a well-planned strategy that covers pricing, logistics, compliance, and risk management.

Choosing the Right Trade Approach

Exporters broadly have two approaches when supplying rice to Nigeria. The first is direct shipment into Nigerian ports under the current duty structure. The second involves routing cargo through neighboring countries, particularly Benin, which has historically been used as an alternative entry point.

With the recent duty reductions, direct exports to Nigeria are becoming more viable than before. This reduces dependency on indirect routes and allows for better transparency in pricing and documentation. However, the indirect route through Benin may still remain relevant in certain cases, depending on cost structures and buyer preferences.

That said, traders must be cautious. Authorities are closely monitoring trade flows, and improper routing or documentation issues can lead to complications. It is essential to fully understand current regulations before choosing the most suitable route.

Pricing Strategy and Market Positioning

Pricing will play a decisive role in capturing this opportunity. Nigerian buyers are highly sensitive to price changes, especially in the broken rice segment. Exporters must calculate landed costs carefully, taking into account duties, freight, insurance, port charges, and local distribution expenses.

A competitive price does not always mean the lowest price. Reliability, consistent quality, and clear contract terms can justify slightly higher pricing if they reduce risk for the buyer. Early movers in this market may also benefit from better margins before competition intensifies.

It is also important to stay flexible. As more suppliers enter the market, price dynamics may shift quickly. Exporters who can adapt their pricing strategies in real time will have a stronger advantage.

Logistics and Supply Chain Planning

Efficient logistics can make or break a deal in this market. Nigerian ports can experience congestion, and clearance timelines may vary. Working with experienced freight forwarders and local agents can help minimize delays and ensure smoother operations.

Shipment planning should include realistic timelines, proper documentation, and contingency measures. Exporters should also consider partial shipments or staggered deliveries to reduce risk exposure, especially in a volatile policy environment.

Another key factor is packaging and quality control. Rice shipments must meet buyer specifications consistently. Any deviation can lead to disputes, delays, or financial losses.

Contract Structuring and Risk Mitigation

Given the fluid policy environment, contracts should be structured with strong safeguards. This includes clear terms on pricing validity, delivery timelines, payment conditions, and responsibilities in case of regulatory changes.

Including clauses that address duty revisions or unforeseen policy changes can help protect both parties. Payment security is equally important, and exporters should prefer structured payment mechanisms that reduce financial risk.

Due diligence on buyers is essential. Working with verified and experienced importers can significantly reduce the chances of disputes or defaults.

Moving from Opportunity to Execution

The Nigerian rice market is not just about identifying demand. It is about converting that demand into successful transactions. Exporters who combine speed with careful planning will be better positioned to navigate uncertainties.

This is a market where preparation meets timing. Acting too slowly may result in missed opportunities, while acting without preparation can lead to avoidable risks.

In the final part, we will summarize the overall opportunity, highlight key takeaways, and provide a clear strategic outlook for exporters looking to capitalize on this evolving trade window.

Nigeria Rice Trade Window 2026: Key Takeaways and Strategic Outlook for Exporters

As the Nigerian government reshapes its import policy to address rising food inflation, the global rice trade has been presented with a rare and time-sensitive opportunity. This is not a routine market shift. It is a strategic window that requires both urgency and discipline from exporters who are looking to expand their footprint in West Africa.

A Clear but Short-Term Opportunity

The reduction in import duties has immediately improved the commercial viability of rice exports to Nigeria. For the first time in years, direct trade into one of Africa’s largest consumption markets is becoming practical under formal channels.

However, it is important to recognize that this is not a permanent policy transformation. The Nigerian government’s primary objective is to stabilize domestic prices and ensure food availability. Once these goals are achieved, there is a strong possibility that duties or restrictions could be revised again.

This makes timing one of the most critical factors. Exporters who move quickly and strategically are more likely to secure profitable deals and establish market presence before conditions change.

First-Mover Advantage in a Competitive Market

Early participation in this trade window offers several advantages. Exporters who enter the market now can build relationships with key importers, understand buyer preferences, and position themselves as reliable suppliers.

In emerging or reopening markets, trust is often as valuable as price. Buyers tend to continue working with partners who demonstrate consistency and professionalism during initial transactions. This creates an opportunity not just for short-term profits, but also for long-term business potential.

At the same time, competition is expected to increase as more exporters recognize the opportunity. This will gradually put pressure on pricing and margins, making early entry even more beneficial.

The Role of TIC in Risk-Controlled Trade Execution

In a dynamic and policy-sensitive market like Nigeria, the role of the TIC (Testing, Inspection, and Certification) industry becomes increasingly important. Ensuring that shipments meet quality standards, contractual specifications, and regulatory requirements is critical for avoiding disputes, delays, or financial losses.

Independent inspection, pre-shipment verification, and quality assurance processes help both exporters and importers build trust and reduce operational risk. In markets where policies can change quickly, having proper inspection and certification support adds an extra layer of security to transactions.

Organizations such as TIC Quality Control, operating within the TIC ecosystem, play a key role in supporting exporters with inspection, compliance, and quality control services aligned with international trade standards.

Balancing Speed with Risk Management

While speed is important, it should not come at the cost of proper risk management. The Nigerian market, in its current state, requires careful execution.

Exporters must stay updated with the latest import regulations and ensure full compliance at every stage of the transaction. Even small documentation errors can lead to delays or financial losses.

Contracts should be structured to account for uncertainties, including possible duty changes or policy adjustments. Clear communication with buyers and logistics partners is essential to avoid misunderstandings and ensure smooth operations.

Financial planning is equally important. Currency fluctuations, payment security, and cost variations must all be considered when finalizing deals.

Final Thoughts

The message is simple: the window is open, but timing is critical.

Nigeria’s decision to reduce rice import duties has created immediate demand and renewed trade potential. For exporters, this is a chance to re-enter a high-volume market under more favorable conditions.

At the same time, the environment remains dynamic. Policies can change, risks remain, and execution challenges must be managed carefully.

Those who combine timely action with informed decision-making, supported by strong compliance and inspection frameworks, will be best positioned to turn this opportunity into measurable business growth.

Understanding Battery Categories in Export Trade

Before getting into regulations, it is important to clearly understand the types of batteries commonly exported to Egypt. Each category has different compliance and safety requirements.

1. Dry Batteries

Dry batteries are widely used in everyday consumer products such as remote controls, flashlights, toys, and small electronic devices.

Common types include:

  • Alkaline batteries
  • Zinc-carbon batteries

These batteries are considered lower risk compared to lithium batteries, but they still require quality checks and compliance with chemical safety regulations. Poor quality dry batteries can leak, damage products, and harm brand reputation.

2. Lithium Batteries

Lithium batteries are highly popular due to their efficiency and long life. They are used in:

  • Mobile phones
  • Laptops
  • Power banks
  • Electric vehicles

However, they are classified as dangerous goods during transportation because they can overheat, catch fire, or explode if not handled properly.

Because of this, lithium batteries require strict testing and certification before export.

3. Lead-Acid Batteries

These are mainly used in:

  • Automotive applications
  • Industrial backup systems
  • Solar energy storage

They are heavier and involve chemical hazards such as acid leakage. Exporting these batteries requires proper handling, packaging, and compliance checks.

Many exporters underestimate the importance of compliance when entering the Egyptian market. In reality, Egypt has strict import control systems to ensure product safety, environmental protection, and consumer safety.

The General Organization for Export and Import Control plays a key role in regulating imported goods, including batteries.

1. Avoid Shipment Rejection

If your shipment does not meet Egyptian standards or lacks required documentation, it can be rejected at the port.

2. Ensure Product Safety

Batteries are sensitive products. Faulty batteries can cause fires, leaks, or damage, leading to serious risks.

3. Build Trust with Buyers

Egyptian importers prefer suppliers who follow proper testing and certification processes. It builds long-term business relationships.

4. Meet Environmental Regulations

Certain chemicals like mercury and cadmium are restricted in batteries. Non-compliance can lead to penalties.

Key Standards for Battery Export

Exporters must follow international testing and safety standards to ensure smooth clearance and safe transportation.

One of the most important standards is:

  • UN 38.3

This standard is mandatory for lithium batteries and ensures they can safely withstand transport conditions such as vibration, temperature changes, and impact.

Another important standard is:

  • IEC 62133

This standard focuses on the safety of rechargeable batteries used in portable devices.

These certifications are not just formalities. They are essential documents that prove your product is safe and compliant for international trade.

Documentation Required for Exporting Batteries to Egypt

Accurate documentation is one of the most common challenges exporters face. Even small errors can delay shipments.

Here are the key documents required:

  • Commercial invoice
  • Packing list
  • Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS)
  • UN38.3 test report and summary
  • Product specifications
  • Certificate of conformity if required

Additionally, Egypt operates under an advanced cargo system where shipments must be registered before arrival. Exporters must coordinate closely with importers to ensure all documentation is correctly submitted.

Working with a reliable TIC service provider ensures that every aspect of the shipment is verified before it leaves the origin country.

Setting the Foundation for Successful Export

In the next part, we will go deeper into testing procedures, common mistakes exporters make, and how professional TIC services in Egypt can help ensure smooth and successful market entry.

Batteries & Dry Batteries Export to Egypt: Testing, Risks, and How to Ensure Compliance 

Battery Testing Procedures Every Exporter Must Understand

When exporting batteries to Egypt, testing is not just a technical requirement. It is a critical step that determines whether your shipment will be accepted or rejected.

Different types of batteries require different testing methods, but the goal is always the same: to ensure safety, reliability, and compliance with international and Egyptian regulations.

1. Performance and Capacity Testing

This test checks whether the battery performs as claimed.

It evaluates:

  • Energy capacity
  • Discharge rate
  • Efficiency over time

For dry batteries, this ensures they deliver consistent power. For lithium batteries, it confirms long-term usability and stability.

2. Thermal and Safety Testing

Temperature is one of the biggest risk factors in batteries.

Thermal testing evaluates how a battery behaves under:

  • High temperatures
  • Rapid temperature changes
  • Overheating conditions

This is especially important for lithium batteries, which can become dangerous if not properly tested.

3. Short Circuit and Overcharge Testing

These tests simulate real-world risks.

They check:

  • What happens if the battery is short-circuited
  • How it reacts to overcharging

A compliant battery should not explode, leak, or catch fire under these conditions.

4. Leakage Testing for Dry Batteries

Even though dry batteries are considered lower risk, leakage is a common issue.

Leakage testing ensures:

  • No chemical escape
  • Proper sealing
  • Safe usage in consumer products

This is crucial for maintaining product quality and avoiding customer complaints.

5. Transport Simulation Tests

To comply with UN 38.3, batteries must pass transport-related tests such as:

  • Vibration testing
  • Shock testing
  • Altitude simulation
  • Impact resistance

These tests ensure the battery can survive shipping conditions without becoming hazardous.

Packaging and Labeling Requirements

Even if your product passes testing, improper packaging can still cause shipment rejection.

Battery exports to Egypt must follow strict packaging and labeling rules, especially for lithium batteries.

Key packaging requirements:

  • Strong, durable outer packaging
  • Protection against short circuits
  • Separation of battery terminals
  • Shock-resistant cushioning

Labeling requirements include:

  • Battery type identification
  • Hazard labels for lithium batteries
  • Handling instructions
  • Manufacturer details

Incorrect or missing labels are one of the most common reasons shipments get delayed or stopped at customs.

Common Challenges Exporters Face

Many exporters run into problems not because of bad products, but due to lack of awareness or poor preparation.

At the same time, carriers are deliberately avoiding direct transit through the Strait of Hormuz due to ongoing regional risks. Instead, they are implementing alternative routing strategies to maintain supply chain continuity.

For exporters dealing with Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, these changes introduce new operational considerations that must be understood and managed effectively.

What Has Changed in Upper Gulf Shipping?

Traditionally, cargo destined for the Upper Gulf would move directly through the Strait of Hormuz. This route has long been the primary maritime corridor connecting global shipping networks to Gulf ports.

The current situation reflects a different approach. Shipping lines have resumed services but are relying on a combination of:

  • Third-party feeder vessels
  • Regional transshipment hubs
  • Bonded land transportation

This shift represents a structural adjustment in logistics operations rather than a temporary workaround.

Why Are Carriers Avoiding the Strait of Hormuz?

The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most strategically important shipping routes in the world. However, it is also highly sensitive to geopolitical developments.

To mitigate risk and ensure uninterrupted cargo flow, carriers are choosing to:

  • Reduce exposure to high-risk maritime zones
  • Maintain operational continuity through alternative routing
  • Protect cargo, vessels, and crew

This strategy allows trade to continue, even under uncertain regional conditions.

How the New Routing System Works

The revised logistics model involves multiple stages instead of a single direct shipping route.

Cargo is first transported to regional hubs such as Sharjah. From there, it is redistributed using feeder services and land transport connections. A key component of this system is bonded trucking between Sharjah and Khorfakkan, which typically takes approximately five days.

From these connection points, feeder vessels serve Upper Gulf destinations including Iraq, Kuwait, Dammam in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates.

While effective, this system introduces additional coordination and complexity compared to traditional direct shipping routes.

Key Operational Considerations

Exporters and logistics planners must take several factors into account when working within this updated framework.

Irregular Scheduling

Feeder vessel operations are not running on fixed weekly schedules. Instead, they are influenced by regional safety conditions and operational constraints. This can result in variability in departure and arrival times.

Extended Transit Times

The use of transshipment and land transport adds extra steps to the logistics chain. As a result, overall transit times may be longer than before.

Cargo Limitations

The current setup supports dry cargo, reefer cargo, and in-gauge special cargo. Out-of-gauge shipments may require alternative arrangements or additional planning.

Alternative Routing Options

Carrier’s Haulage solutions via Jeddah remain available and can serve as an additional option depending on shipment requirements.

Impact on Exporters to Iraq

Exporters to Iraq should pay particular attention to these developments. In addition to logistical complexity, shipments to Iraq require strict compliance with regulatory requirements.

These often include:

  • Certificate of Conformity (CoC)
  • Product inspection and verification
  • Accurate documentation for customs clearance

With routing becoming more complex, any errors in compliance or documentation can lead to delays, increased costs, or rejected shipments.

Cost and Planning Implications

The new routing model may influence overall logistics costs. Exporters should consider:

  • Additional handling and transshipment charges
  • Potential increases in freight rates
  • Costs associated with extended transit times

Careful planning and cost assessment are essential to maintaining profitability and delivery reliability.

A Shift in Supply Chain Strategy

This development highlights a broader trend in global logistics. Supply chains are increasingly being designed with flexibility and risk management in mind.

Rather than relying on a single critical route, companies are adopting diversified logistics strategies that can adapt to changing conditions.

This shift emphasizes:

  • Resilience over efficiency alone
  • Multi-modal transport solutions
  • Proactive risk mitigation

For exporters, this means adjusting expectations and planning processes accordingly.

How Businesses Can Adapt

To navigate this evolving landscape, businesses should focus on the following:

  • Plan shipments earlier to accommodate variability
  • Maintain close communication with logistics partners
  • Ensure all documentation is accurate and complete
  • Build flexibility into supply chain operations

These steps can help reduce disruptions and maintain consistent cargo flow.

The Role of TICQC

TICQC supports exporters by providing reliable compliance and inspection services, particularly for shipments to Iraq.

Our services include:

  • Certificate of Conformity (CoC) issuance
  • Product inspection and verification
  • Guidance on regulatory requirements

In an environment where logistics operations are becoming more complex, ensuring compliance is critical to avoiding delays and maintaining smooth trade flows.

Conclusion

The reopening of Upper Gulf shipping routes is a positive development, but it does not represent a return to previous operating conditions.

By avoiding direct transit through the Strait of Hormuz and adopting alternative routing strategies, carriers are prioritizing continuity and risk management.

Exporters must adapt to this new environment by planning more carefully, maintaining flexibility, and ensuring full compliance with regulatory requirements.

As global logistics continues to evolve, businesses that respond proactively to these changes will be better positioned to maintain efficiency and competitiveness in international trade.
